passages.q: Why might investors care more about others’ opinions than about true value?
p: In his General Theory of 1936, John Maynard Keynes compared professional investment to a newspaper competition in which entrants had to pick the six prettiest faces from a hundred photographs, the prize going to the entrant whose choices came closest to the average choices of all entrants; to win, each competitor should select not the faces they personally found prettiest, nor even those they thought others would find prettiest, but those they expected others to expect others to choose, and so on through further degrees of anticipation.

Keynes’s point was that in markets where short-term trading dominates, prices can be driven less by estimates of an asset’s long-term value than by estimates of how other participants will behave, so that a rational investor might buy an asset they believe is overvalued if they expect others to buy it from them at a higher price. Economists have tested versions of this reasoning in experiments, such as asking people to choose a number that is two-thirds of the average of everyone’s choices, and found that most people reason only a step or two ahead, rather than following the logic to its conclusion.

The insight helps explain bubbles, in which prices rise far above any plausible fundamental value because each buyer expects to sell to someone else, and also momentum, in which trends persist because participants anticipate that others will follow them. It carries a lesson beyond finance: in any situation where outcomes depend on coordination, from fashion to technology standards, success depends on understanding not only what is good but what others will believe is good, and on how many steps ahead they are likely to think.
g: Keynes likened investing to a beauty contest won by predicting others’ average choice, which requires anticipating their anticipations.
In short-term markets, prices depend on expected behaviour more than long-term value, though experiments show people reason only a step or two ahead.
This explains bubbles and momentum, and in any coordination setting success depends on predicting what others will believe is good.
k: Keynes’s beauty contest: winners pick what they expect others to expect others to choose.
Short-term prices reflect expected behaviour more than value; experiments show people reason only one or two steps ahead.
Explains bubbles and momentum; in coordination settings, predict others’ beliefs as well as quality.

passages.q: How can a central bank influence the economy simply by what it says?
p: Central banks traditionally influenced the economy by changing short-term interest rates, but the effect of a rate change depends heavily on what people expect future rates to be, since long-term borrowing costs, from mortgages to corporate bonds, reflect anticipated rates over many years. Increasingly, central banks have tried to shape those expectations directly, by communicating their intentions, a practice known as forward guidance.

When short-term rates fell close to zero after the 2008 financial crisis, leaving little room for further cuts, forward guidance became a principal tool: by promising to keep rates low for an extended period, or until conditions such as unemployment improved, central banks aimed to lower long-term rates and encourage borrowing and investment immediately. Its success depends on credibility; if markets doubt that the bank will keep its word, the guidance has little effect, and if the bank later reverses course, it may damage the trust on which future guidance relies.

The approach reflects a broader shift in how economists think about policy, in which expectations are not merely a background condition but a lever. A central bank widely believed to be committed to low inflation may find that inflation stays low partly because firms and workers expect it to, setting prices and wages accordingly, whereas one whose commitment is doubted may need much harsher actions to achieve the same result. Words, in this sense, can substitute for actions, but only if they have been backed by actions often enough to be believed.
g: Rate changes work through expected future rates, so central banks increasingly shape expectations through forward guidance.
Near zero rates after 2008 made guidance a main tool to lower long-term rates, but it depends on credibility and trust.
Expectations are now a lever, so credible banks keep inflation low more easily, but words work only when backed by past actions.
k: Long-term rates reflect expected future rates, so central banks communicate intentions: forward guidance.

passages.q: What did India’s Goods and Services Tax change, and what did it cost?
p: Before 2017, goods moving across India faced a tangle of central and state taxes, with different rates and rules in each state, checkpoints at state borders where trucks could wait for hours or days, and taxes levied on taxes as products moved through supply chains. Economists had long argued that this fragmentation turned a single country into many small markets and discouraged investment in efficient national logistics.

The Goods and Services Tax, introduced in July 2017 after years of negotiation between the central government and the states, replaced many of these levies with a single destination-based tax administered jointly, with credits for tax paid at earlier stages so that tax was not charged repeatedly on the same value. A constitutional amendment created a council of central and state finance ministers to set rates, an unusual experiment in cooperative federalism, since states surrendered significant independent taxing power in exchange for a share of the common pool and compensation for revenue losses during a transition.

The early years were difficult. Multiple rate bands, frequent changes and complex compliance requirements burdened small businesses, and disputes arose over compensation when revenues fell short. Over time, collections grew, interstate checkpoints largely disappeared and logistics times fell, though debates continue over simplifying the rate structure and over how much fiscal autonomy states gave up. The reform illustrates how integrating a large internal market can require sacrifices of sovereignty, as well as patient correction of initial design flaws.
g: Before 2017, India’s goods faced tangled central and state taxes, border checkpoints and cascading taxes, fragmenting the market.
GST replaced them with one destination-based tax with credits, run by a joint council, so states traded taxing power for a common pool.
Early complexity burdened small firms, but collections grew and checkpoints vanished, showing integration needs sovereignty sacrifices and correction.
k: Pre-2017 India had fragmented, cascading taxes and border checkpoints.
GST (July 2017): a single destination-based tax with input credits, set by a joint central–state council.

passages.q: What is quantitative easing, and did it work?
p: When the 2008 financial crisis drove short-term interest rates close to zero, central banks in the United States, Britain and elsewhere turned to quantitative easing: creating new central bank money electronically and using it to buy large quantities of government bonds and, in some cases, other assets. By increasing demand for these assets, central banks pushed up their prices and pushed down long-term interest rates, aiming to make borrowing cheaper, support asset values and encourage spending when conventional policy had run out of room.

The policy was expanded on an enormous scale, again during the pandemic in 2020, and research generally suggests that it lowered long-term borrowing costs and helped stabilise financial markets at moments of panic, though estimates of its effects on growth and employment vary widely. Fears that it would cause runaway inflation did not materialise in the decade after 2008, largely because much of the new money remained as reserves within the banking system rather than circulating in the wider economy.

Quantitative easing also had side effects that remain contested. By raising the prices of bonds, shares and property, it disproportionately benefited people who already owned such assets, a distributional consequence critics argue widened wealth inequality. It left central banks holding vast portfolios, exposed to losses when interest rates rose sharply in 2022 and 2023, and blurred the line between monetary policy and government financing. The episode shows how a tool introduced as an emergency measure can become a routine instrument before its long-run consequences are fully understood.
g: With rates near zero after 2008, central banks created money to buy bonds, lowering long-term rates to encourage borrowing and spending.
Research suggests it lowered borrowing costs and calmed markets, and feared inflation did not follow because much money stayed as bank reserves.

passages.t: The window of the demographic dividend
passages.q: Why does a country’s age structure matter so much for its growth?
p: As countries develop, death rates usually fall first and birth rates later, so that for several decades the population contains an unusually large share of working-age adults relative to children and the elderly. Economists call the potential boost to growth during this period the demographic dividend: with fewer dependants per worker, households can save more, governments can invest more per child in education and health, and the expanding labour force can raise output, provided there are productive jobs for it.

East Asian economies, including South Korea and Taiwan, are often cited as having harvested this dividend effectively in the late twentieth century, combining a bulge in working-age population with heavy investment in education and export-oriented manufacturing that absorbed young workers. India is now in the midst of its own window, with a large and young labour force and a median age under thirty, though the window will narrow over the coming decades as fertility falls and the population ages.

The dividend is not automatic. If young people cannot find productive work, a large working-age population can mean unemployment, underemployment and frustration rather than growth; if women’s participation in paid work remains low, much of the potential labour force is untapped. Meanwhile, countries further along the path, such as Japan and much of Europe, face the reverse challenge of shrinking workforces supporting growing numbers of retirees. Demography sets the opportunity; policy on education, jobs and participation determines whether it is taken.

East Asian economies harvested it with education and export jobs, and India is now in its window with a young workforce.

passages.q: How might we decide what a fair society looks like if we did not know our place in it?
p: In A Theory of Justice, published in 1971, the philosopher John Rawls proposed a thought experiment for identifying fair principles of social organisation: imagine choosing the basic rules of a society from behind a veil of ignorance, not knowing whether you would be born rich or poor, talented or not, into a favoured or a disadvantaged group. Because no one could tailor the rules to their own advantage, Rawls argued, the principles chosen would be fair to all.

Rawls concluded that people in this position would choose, first, equal basic liberties for everyone and, second, what he called the difference principle: social and economic inequalities would be permitted only if they worked to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged members of society and were attached to positions open to all under fair equality of opportunity. Inequality, on this view, is not wrong in itself; higher pay for doctors might be justified if it draws talent into medicine in ways that benefit everyone, including the worst off.

Critics challenged the framework from several directions. The philosopher Robert Nozick argued in 1974 that justice concerns how holdings arose, through voluntary exchange and legitimate acquisition, rather than whether outcomes match a pattern; others questioned whether people behind the veil would really be as cautious as Rawls assumed, rather than gambling on better positions. Yet the veil of ignorance remains one of the most widely used tools for testing intuitions about fairness, because it forces a simple question: would you accept this rule if you did not know which side of it you would be on?
g: Rawls proposed choosing society’s rules behind a veil of ignorance about one’s own position, so no one could rig them.
He argued people would choose equal liberties and the difference principle, allowing inequalities only if they benefit the least advantaged.
Nozick and others challenged it, but the veil endures as a test: would you accept this rule not knowing your side of it?
k: Rawls (1971): choose society’s rules behind a veil of ignorance about your own position.

passages.q: How can self-sacrificing behaviour evolve if natural selection favours survival?
p: Altruism, behaviour that benefits others at a cost to oneself, posed a puzzle for evolutionary theory: if natural selection favours traits that help individuals survive and reproduce, how could traits that reduce an individual’s own chances persist? Worker bees that never reproduce and sting intruders at the cost of their lives seemed especially hard to explain.

In 1964 the biologist W. D. Hamilton proposed an answer based on genes rather than individuals. Relatives share a proportion of their genes by descent, half between parent and child or full siblings, an eighth between first cousins, so a gene that leads an individual to help relatives can spread if the benefit to the relatives, weighted by relatedness, exceeds the cost to the helper. The condition, known as Hamilton’s rule, explained why altruism is directed preferentially towards kin, a pattern observed widely in nature, and offered an account of the unusual social structures of some insects.

Kin selection is not the only route to cooperation. Reciprocity, in which help is returned over repeated interactions, can sustain cooperation among unrelated individuals, and in humans, reputation, social norms and institutions extend cooperation to strangers on a scale unmatched elsewhere in nature. The interplay of these mechanisms helps explain both the remarkable cooperativeness of human societies and the persistent tendency to favour family and in-groups, which institutions of fairness are often designed to counterbalance.
g: Altruism puzzled evolutionary theory because helping others at one’s own cost seems to reduce survival, as worker bees show.
Hamilton showed genes for helping relatives can spread if benefit weighted by relatedness exceeds cost, explaining kin-directed altruism.

passages.t: How the brain cleans at night
passages.q: Does sleep help the brain clear out waste?
p: The brain consumes a large share of the body’s energy and produces metabolic waste, including proteins that can accumulate in harmful ways, yet it lacks the conventional lymphatic vessels that clear waste from other tissues. In 2012 and 2013, the neuroscientist Maiken Nedergaard and colleagues described a system, which they named the glymphatic system, in which cerebrospinal fluid flows along channels surrounding blood vessels and through brain tissue, carrying waste away.

Their experiments in mice suggested that this clearance was far more active during sleep than during wakefulness, in part because the spaces between brain cells appeared to expand during sleep, allowing fluid to flow more freely. Among the substances cleared was beta-amyloid, a protein that accumulates in the brains of people with Alzheimer’s disease. The findings offered a striking hypothesis for one function of sleep: housekeeping that the waking brain is too busy to perform.

The picture is still being refined. Some later studies have questioned aspects of how fluid moves through brain tissue and whether clearance truly increases during sleep, and most direct evidence comes from animals rather than humans. Research in people has found that even a single night of sleep deprivation can raise levels of beta-amyloid in the brain, consistent with the hypothesis but not proof of it. What remains well established is that sleep serves several essential functions, from memory consolidation to metabolic regulation, and that chronic shortage carries real costs.
g: The brain produces waste but lacks normal lymphatic vessels, and Nedergaard described a glymphatic system that flushes waste with fluid.
Mouse studies suggested clearance, including of beta-amyloid, is much more active during sleep, offering a housekeeping role for sleep.

passages.t: The system that pegged the world to the dollar
passages.q: How was the post-war international monetary system designed, and why did it end?
p: In July 1944, delegates from forty-four Allied countries met at Bretton Woods in New Hampshire to design a monetary order that would avoid the competitive devaluations and trade wars of the 1930s. Under the system they created, other currencies were pegged to the US dollar at fixed but adjustable rates, and the dollar was convertible into gold at thirty-five dollars an ounce for foreign governments; the International Monetary Fund and what became the World Bank were established to support the arrangement.

The system underpinned a period of rapid growth and expanding trade, but it contained a tension identified by the economist Robert Triffin: the world needed a growing supply of dollars for trade and reserves, which required the United States to run deficits, yet those deficits steadily eroded confidence that the dollar could be converted into gold at the fixed price. By the late 1960s, foreign holdings of dollars far exceeded American gold reserves, and pressure mounted as countries exchanged dollars for gold.

In August 1971 President Richard Nixon suspended the dollar’s convertibility into gold, and by 1973 major currencies were floating, their values set largely by markets. The end of Bretton Woods did not end the dollar’s central role, which persists in trade, finance and reserves, but it ushered in an era of flexible exchange rates and independent monetary policies. The episode remains a case study in how a system can be undermined by the very success that requires it to expand.

It supported growth, but Triffin showed the world’s need for dollars required US deficits that eroded faith in gold convertibility.

passages.t: What we mean beyond what we say
passages.q: How do listeners understand more than speakers literally say?
p: If a colleague asks whether a candidate was good and you reply that he was very punctual, your listener will probably conclude that he was not good, even though you said nothing negative. The philosopher Paul Grice explained such inferences by proposing that conversation rests on a cooperative principle, and that speakers are expected to follow maxims: to give as much information as needed and no more, to say what they believe true, to be relevant and to be clear.

Listeners assume these maxims are being followed and interpret apparent violations as meaningful, a process Grice called implicature. Praising only punctuality, when asked about overall quality, conspicuously gives less information than required, so the listener infers that nothing better could be said. Likewise, if someone says some of the results were positive, listeners infer that not all were, because if all had been, the speaker would presumably have said so.

The framework has practical force for anyone who speaks or writes at work. Audiences read meaning into what is omitted, emphasised or placed first, so an update that opens with minor successes before mentioning a serious problem may be heard as evasive, and a recommendation hedged with excessive caveats may be heard as lack of conviction. Effective communicators manage implicature deliberately, saying the main point plainly, ordering information by importance and remembering that silence about something will itself be interpreted.

passages.q: What makes a speaker persuasive, according to the oldest theory of rhetoric?
p: In his Rhetoric, written in the fourth century BCE, Aristotle identified three modes of persuasion that a speaker can supply: ethos, persuasion through the speaker’s character, when the speech is delivered in such a way as to make the speaker seem credible, competent and well-intentioned; pathos, persuasion through the audience’s emotions, by putting listeners into a frame of mind receptive to the argument; and logos, persuasion through the argument itself, by demonstrating that something is true or probable.

Aristotle regarded logos as the core of rhetoric but insisted that all three matter, since audiences are not purely rational and do not judge arguments independently of who makes them or how they feel. A strong argument from a speaker the audience distrusts may fail, while an emotionally stirring appeal without substance may persuade in the moment but collapse under scrutiny. Modern research on persuasion broadly echoes the framework, finding that perceived expertise and trustworthiness, emotional resonance and the quality of arguments each influence attitudes, with their relative importance depending on how motivated and able the audience is to think carefully.

For executives, the framework suggests a checklist rather than a formula. Ethos is built before the speech as much as during it, through a record of reliability and candour, and within it through evident preparation and honest acknowledgement of uncertainty. Pathos lies less in theatrical appeals than in connecting a proposal to what the audience actually cares about. Logos requires a clear claim, sound evidence and anticipated objections. Neglecting any one of the three tends to weaken the other two.

passages.q: Which psychological principles make people say yes, and how robust is the evidence?
p: In his 1984 book Influence, the psychologist Robert Cialdini described six principles that, drawing on experiments and on observation of salespeople, fundraisers and advertisers, reliably increase compliance with requests: reciprocity, the urge to return favours; commitment and consistency, the desire to act in line with earlier statements; social proof, the tendency to follow what others do; liking, the greater willingness to agree with people we like; authority, deference to experts; and scarcity, the extra value attached to things that are rare or running out. He later added unity, the sense of shared identity.

The principles have been widely applied. Hotels found that guests were more likely to reuse towels when told that most previous guests in the same room had done so; tax authorities in Britain raised payment rates by telling late payers that most people in their area had already paid. Such findings show how small changes in wording, built on social proof or commitment, can shift behaviour at scale and at little cost.

Two cautions apply. Some effects are smaller or less consistent than early studies suggested, and results vary by context, so persuasion techniques are better treated as hypotheses to test than as guaranteed levers. And the same principles can be used manipulatively, through fake scarcity, invented testimonials or pressure that exploits obligation, which damages trust once discovered. Cialdini himself drew a line between using principles that are genuinely present, such as pointing to real popularity or real expertise, and manufacturing them, which he regarded as both unethical and, over time, self-defeating.

passages.q: Why do negotiators so often miss deals that would leave both sides better off?
p: Negotiation researchers distinguish between distributive bargaining, in which parties divide a fixed amount, so that one side’s gain is the other’s loss, and integrative bargaining, in which they create value by finding trades that serve both sides’ interests. Many real negotiations involve several issues, such as price, delivery date, payment terms and warranty, that the parties value differently, which creates room to trade concessions on issues one side values less for gains on issues it values more.

Yet experiments consistently find that negotiators leave much of this potential value unrealised. One reason, identified by researchers such as Max Bazerman and Margaret Neale, is the fixed-pie bias: the assumption that the other side’s interests are directly opposed to one’s own on every issue, so that anything they want must come at one’s expense. Negotiators also tend to bargain issue by issue, settling price before discussing terms, which prevents trades across issues, and they withhold information about priorities for fear of being exploited.

Practical techniques can counter these tendencies: discussing several issues together rather than sequentially, asking questions about the other side’s priorities and sharing some of one’s own, proposing multiple packages of equal value to oneself and observing which the other side prefers, and separating the creation of value from its division. Integrative bargaining does not eliminate competition, since the enlarged pie must still be divided, but it ensures there is more to divide.
g: Distributive bargaining splits a fixed amount, while integrative bargaining creates value by trading issues the sides value differently.
Negotiators leave value unrealised through the fixed-pie bias, issue-by-issue bargaining and withholding priorities.
Discussing issues together, sharing priorities and offering equal-value packages help, so there is more to divide.
k: Distributive bargaining divides a fixed pie; integrative bargaining creates value by trading differently valued issues.
Fixed-pie bias, sequential issue-by-issue bargaining and secrecy about priorities leave value on the table.
Negotiate issues together, exchange priorities, offer equal-value packages; then divide the larger pie.

mc.s: What is the main lesson?
o: Many negotiations can create value by trading across issues, if negotiators avoid common biases
mc.e: The passage builds to this lesson.

mc.s: Why does bargaining issue by issue destroy value?
o: It prevents trades that give up a less valued issue for a more valued one

mc.s: Which tactic best uncovers integrative potential?
o: Offering two packages that are equally good for you and seeing which the other side prefers
Making one final offer on price
mc.e: The third paragraph recommends multiple equal-value packages.

v.d: A concession is something yielded to reach agreement.
Unrealised value is potential that was never captured.

passages.q: Is it better to control an entire ecosystem or to open it to others?
p: Technology platforms face a recurring choice between closed, integrated ecosystems, in which one company controls the hardware, software and distribution, and open approaches, in which components are made by many firms and standards are shared. Apple’s smartphone business exemplifies the first, designing its own chips, devices and operating system and controlling which apps can be distributed through its store; Google’s Android, licensed to many manufacturers, exemplifies a more open model, though Google retains control over key services.

Each approach has distinctive advantages. Integration allows tight optimisation across components, consistent user experience, stronger security controls and the capture of value at several layers; Apple has earned a large share of the smartphone industry’s profits despite selling a minority of the units. Openness spreads adoption faster through many partners and price points, encourages variety and can make a platform the default standard; Android runs on most of the world’s smartphones.

The trade-offs shift over time. Closed systems risk slower adoption and regulatory pressure as their control becomes a bottleneck for others, as app-store rules have drawn scrutiny in Europe and elsewhere; open systems risk fragmentation, inconsistent quality and difficulty capturing value, since partners may commoditise the platform. Many successful strategies are hybrids, open where breadth matters and controlled where quality and economics depend on it. The question for any platform is which layers to own and which to share, a choice that defines both its reach and its margins.
g: Platforms choose between closed integration, like Apple controlling hardware, software and distribution, and openness, like licensed Android.
Integration brings optimisation, security and profit capture, while openness brings faster adoption, variety and default-standard status.
Closed systems face slower adoption and regulation, open ones fragmentation and weak capture, so many choose hybrids: which layers to own.
k: Closed ecosystems (Apple) control many layers; open ones (Android) license to many partners.
Integration: optimisation, security, profit capture; openness: adoption, variety, standard-setting.
Closed risks regulation and slow adoption; open risks fragmentation; hybrids decide which layers to own.

o: Which layers to own and which to share

mc.s: How can Apple earn most industry profits with a minority of units?
o: Integration lets it capture value across several layers at premium prices
It sells more phones than anyone

mc.e: The third paragraph lists these risks.

passages.q: Why did AI researchers come to believe that scale itself drives capability?
p: In 2020 researchers at OpenAI, led by Jared Kaplan, reported that the performance of language models improved predictably as three quantities increased: the number of model parameters, the amount of training data and the amount of computation used for training. Across many orders of magnitude, the relationship followed smooth power laws, meaning that each increase in scale produced a consistent, if diminishing, improvement in how well models predicted text.

These scaling laws shaped investment across the industry, since they suggested that capability could be bought, at least in part, with more computing power and data. In 2022 a team at DeepMind refined the picture in a study often called the Chinchilla paper, finding that many large models had been undertrained relative to their size and that, for a fixed budget of computation, models should be smaller and trained on considerably more data than had been common. A model built on that principle outperformed larger predecessors.

Scaling laws describe trends in predictive loss rather than guaranteeing specific abilities, and some capabilities have appeared relatively abruptly as models grew, while others have improved only slowly. Researchers debate how far the trends will continue, given limits on high-quality data, the cost and energy of computation, and the possibility that new methods, such as training models to reason at length before answering, may matter as much as raw scale. The laws nonetheless illustrate a broader lesson about technology strategy: where returns to investment are predictable, the competition shifts towards whoever can secure the inputs.
g: Kaplan’s team found language model performance improves predictably with parameters, data and compute, following smooth power laws.
These scaling laws drove investment, and the 2022 Chinchilla study showed many models were undertrained, favouring smaller models with more data.
Scaling predicts loss, not specific abilities, and its limits are debated, but predictable returns shift competition to securing inputs.
k: Scaling laws (Kaplan et al., 2020): performance improves predictably with parameters, data and compute.
Chinchilla (2022): for a fixed compute budget, smaller models trained on more data do better.
Laws predict loss, not specific abilities; limits are debated; predictable returns make competition about inputs.

mc.s: What broader strategic lesson does the passage draw?
o: When returns to investment are predictable, competition shifts to securing inputs

mc.s: What did the Chinchilla finding imply about earlier large models?
o: They used too little training data for their size
mc.e: The second paragraph says many were undertrained.

o: trained on too little data for its size
v.d: An undertrained model has not seen enough data.

passages.t: Why some services keep getting dearer
passages.q: Why do education, healthcare and live performance grow ever more expensive relative to goods?
p: In the 1960s the economists William Baumol and William Bowen observed that a string quartet required the same number of musicians and the same amount of time to perform a piece of Beethoven as it had in the nineteenth century, whereas the labour needed to manufacture cars, clothing or electronics had fallen dramatically. Yet musicians’ wages had risen over time, broadly in line with wages elsewhere, because orchestras had to compete with other employers for talent.

The consequence, now called Baumol’s cost disease, is that the relative cost of labour-intensive services with limited scope for productivity growth rises steadily: as productivity and wages climb in manufacturing, sectors such as education, healthcare, social care and the performing arts must pay higher wages without producing correspondingly more, so their prices increase faster than the average. The phenomenon helps explain why the share of national income spent on such services tends to grow even when their quality or quantity does not change much.

Baumol emphasised that the disease is a sign of overall prosperity rather than of failure, since rising productivity elsewhere makes society richer and better able to afford costly services. It nevertheless creates pressures on public budgets and reasons to seek productivity gains where possible, through technology, better organisation or new ways of delivering services, though such gains must be weighed carefully against quality, since a lecture to a larger audience or a shorter medical appointment raises measured productivity at a potential cost to the outcome.
g: Baumol and Bowen noted a string quartet needs the same labour as centuries ago, while manufacturing labour fell, yet musicians’ wages rose.
So labour-intensive services with little productivity growth get relatively dearer, explaining rising spending on education, healthcare and arts.
It reflects overall prosperity, but strains budgets, so seek productivity gains carefully without sacrificing quality.
k: A string quartet needs as much labour as ever, while manufacturing labour has fallen; wages rise everywhere.
Baumol’s cost disease: low-productivity-growth services become relatively more expensive.
It reflects prosperity but strains budgets; productivity gains must not undermine quality.

mc.s: What does Baumol’s cost disease explain?
o: Why labour-intensive services become relatively more expensive over time

mc.s: Why must orchestras raise wages despite no productivity gain?
o: They compete with other employers whose wages are rising

mc.s: Why should a hospital be cautious about simply shortening appointments to raise productivity?
o: It may raise measured productivity while harming patient outcomes

v.d: Correspondingly means in proportion to something else.
Prosperity is a state of thriving economically.

passages.t: Strategy as a set of choices
passages.q: What separates a real strategy from a list of goals?
p: Many documents called strategies are, on inspection, lists of aspirations, such as becoming the market leader, delighting customers or growing revenue by a certain percentage, combined with initiatives that a company would pursue anyway. In Playing to Win, published in 2013, the former Procter & Gamble chief executive A. G. Lafley and the strategy scholar Roger Martin argued that strategy is instead an integrated set of choices that uniquely positions a firm in its industry so as to create sustainable advantage and superior value.

They framed these choices as five linked questions: what is our winning aspiration; where will we play, in terms of customers, products, channels and geographies; how will we win in those chosen places; what capabilities must be in place; and what management systems are required to support them. The crucial word is choice. Deciding where to play necessarily means deciding where not to play, and a strategy that rules nothing out provides no guidance when resources must be allocated or trade-offs faced.

The framework resonates with a related critique by the strategist Richard Rumelt, who in Good Strategy Bad Strategy, published in 2011, described the kernel of a good strategy as a diagnosis of the challenge, a guiding policy for dealing with it and coherent actions to carry it out, and warned against fluff, failure to face the problem and mistaking goals for strategy. Both accounts point to a simple test: if a competitor could plausibly adopt your stated strategy word for word, or if it makes no difficult trade-offs, it is probably not a strategy at all.
g: Many so-called strategies are lists of aspirations, but Lafley and Martin define strategy as integrated choices creating unique advantage.
Their five questions centre on choice, since deciding where to play means deciding where not to, or the strategy gives no guidance.
Rumelt’s kernel of diagnosis, guiding policy and actions agrees, so if a rival could copy it or it makes no trade-offs, it is not a strategy.
k: Strategy is an integrated set of choices creating unique advantage, not a list of goals (Lafley and Martin, 2013).
Five questions: aspiration, where to play, how to win, capabilities, management systems; choice means saying no.
Rumelt’s kernel: diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent actions; if a rival could copy it, it isn’t a strategy.

mc.s: What is the passage’s test of a real strategy?
o: It makes difficult trade-offs that a competitor could not simply copy
mc.e: The final sentence gives the test.

mc.s: Why does a strategy that rules nothing out fail?
o: It gives no guidance when resources must be allocated

o: “We will serve mid-sized design agencies in Europe with an all-in-one workflow tool, and will not pursue enterprise or consumer markets.”
“We will be the best in our industry.”

v.d: Integrated choices fit together and reinforce one another.
The kernel is the core of something.

passages.q: How did Peter Drucker change thinking about managing professionals?
p: The management writer Peter Drucker, in The Practice of Management of 1954, popularised management by objectives, a process in which managers and employees agree on goals and individuals are given autonomy in deciding how to reach them, judged by results rather than by close supervision of their activities. A few years later he coined the term knowledge worker for people, such as engineers, analysts and teachers, whose principal contribution is applying knowledge rather than manual skill, and predicted that they would become the dominant group in advanced economies.

Drucker argued that knowledge workers could not be managed like factory labour. Their productivity depends on defining the task correctly, which they often understand better than their managers; on autonomy and continuous learning; and on being treated as assets to be developed rather than costs to be controlled. Effectiveness, in his phrase, means doing the right things, which for knowledge workers requires asking what results are needed rather than simply being busy.

Many of Drucker’s ideas became so widely adopted that their origin is forgotten, and some were distorted: management by objectives was often reduced to mechanical target-setting tied to appraisal, the very bureaucracy he warned against. His central questions nonetheless remain sharp for anyone leading professionals: what is the task, what results should it produce, what does this person need in order to produce them, and what should be stopped to make room. Asked honestly, they redirect attention from activity to contribution.
g: Drucker popularised management by objectives, giving people goals and autonomy judged by results, and coined the term knowledge worker.
He argued knowledge workers need correctly defined tasks, autonomy, learning and development, and effectiveness means doing the right things.
His ideas spread and were distorted into mechanical targets, but his questions about task, results and what to stop still redirect focus to contribution.
k: Drucker popularised management by objectives (1954) and coined “knowledge worker”.
Knowledge workers need well-defined tasks, autonomy, learning and development; effectiveness is doing the right things.
MBO was often distorted into bureaucracy; his questions shift focus from activity to contribution.

mc.s: What was Drucker’s key insight about knowledge workers?
o: They must be managed through defined results, autonomy and development rather than close supervision
They should be supervised like factory workers

mc.s: Why was management by objectives often distorted?
o: It was reduced to mechanical target-setting tied to appraisals

mc.s: Which question reflects Drucker’s approach for a new analyst role?
o: “What results should this role produce, and what should we stop doing to make room?”
mc.e: The final paragraph lists these questions.

o: independence to make one’s own decisions
v.d: Autonomy is freedom to act independently.
To redirect attention is to move it elsewhere.

passages.q: Is expertise mostly the result of deliberate practice?
p: In 1993 the psychologist K. Anders Ericsson and colleagues published a study of violinists at a Berlin music academy, finding that the best performers had accumulated far more hours of solitary, deliberate practice, effortful activity designed to improve specific aspects of performance with feedback, than less accomplished peers. The work inspired the popular idea that around ten thousand hours of practice produces mastery, a figure Ericsson himself said was misunderstood, since it was an average rather than a threshold and the type of practice mattered more than the total.

Later research has tested how much practice explains. A 2014 meta-analysis by Brooke Macnamara, David Hambrick and Frederick Oswald, combining many studies, found that deliberate practice was strongly related to performance but accounted for a modest share of the differences between people, around a quarter in games and music, smaller proportions in sports and education, and very little in professions. Factors such as starting age, working memory, personality and opportunity also mattered. Ericsson and others disputed aspects of these analyses, particularly how practice was defined.

Both sides agree on points that are practically useful. Simply accumulating experience does not reliably produce improvement; practice that targets specific weaknesses, at the edge of current ability, with immediate feedback and full concentration, is far more effective than routine repetition. Practice clearly matters, but individuals do not start equal, and the realistic goal of deliberate practice is to become substantially better than one would otherwise be, rather than to guarantee world-class status.
g: Ericsson found top violinists had far more deliberate practice, inspiring the misunderstood 10,000-hour idea.
A 2014 meta-analysis found practice explains a modest share of differences, about a quarter in games and music and less elsewhere, though disputed.
Both sides agree targeted, feedback-rich practice beats repetition, so practice makes people much better but cannot guarantee world-class status.
k: Ericsson (1993): top violinists had more deliberate practice; the 10,000-hour rule is a misunderstanding.
A 2014 meta-analysis found practice explains about a quarter of differences in games and music, less in other fields; disputed.
Targeted, feedback-rich, focused practice beats repetition; it improves you without guaranteeing elite status.

mc.s: What is the passage’s balanced conclusion?
o: Deliberate practice substantially improves performance but does not explain all differences
mc.e: The final paragraph gives this conclusion.

mc.s: Why did Ericsson say the 10,000-hour idea was misunderstood?
o: It was an average, and the kind of practice mattered more than the total

mc.s: Which is deliberate practice for public speaking?
o: Recording a two-minute answer, reviewing one specific weakness and redoing it immediately
Giving the same talk repeatedly without feedback
mc.e: It targets a weakness with feedback and repetition.

v.d: Accumulated hours built up gradually.

o: a level that must be reached
a limit that cannot be passed
v.d: A threshold is a point at which something begins to happen.

passages.q: Why do courts follow past decisions even when judges might decide differently today?
p: In common law systems such as those of England, the United States and India, courts are generally bound to follow the legal principles established in earlier decisions of higher courts, a doctrine known as stare decisis, Latin for to stand by things decided. When a court decides a case, the reasoning necessary to the decision becomes precedent, which lower courts must apply to similar facts, so that the law develops incrementally through accumulated judgments rather than solely through statutes.

The doctrine serves several values. It makes the law predictable, allowing people and businesses to plan their affairs with reasonable confidence about how disputes will be resolved; it promotes equality, in that like cases are treated alike; it restrains individual judges from imposing personal preferences; and it saves effort by not reopening settled questions in every case. Lawyers distinguish between the binding core of a judgment and remarks made in passing, which may be persuasive but do not bind.

Precedent is not absolute. Highest courts can overrule their own earlier decisions when they conclude that a precedent was wrongly decided or has become unworkable, as the United States Supreme Court did in 1954 when it rejected the doctrine of separate but equal in Brown v. Board of Education. Lower courts can distinguish a precedent by showing that the facts before them differ in relevant ways. The tension between stability and correction, between respecting past decisions and fixing their errors, is permanent, and how courts manage it shapes the legitimacy of the law itself.
g: Common law courts follow higher courts’ earlier principles under stare decisis, so law grows incrementally through judgments.
Precedent provides predictability, equality, restraint on judges and efficiency, binding only the core reasoning.
Highest courts can overrule, as in Brown v. Board, and lower courts distinguish, so stability and correction are in permanent tension.
k: Stare decisis: courts follow precedents from higher courts; law develops incrementally.
Precedent gives predictability, equality, judicial restraint and efficiency; only core reasoning binds.
Highest courts can overrule (e.g. Brown v. Board, 1954); stability vs correction is a permanent tension.

mc.s: What tension does the passage identify?
o: Between stability from following precedent and correcting past errors

mc.s: Why does precedent help businesses?
o: It makes the outcome of disputes more predictable for planning

mc.s: How can a lower court avoid applying a precedent?
o: By showing that the facts differ in relevant ways

v.d: Incremental development happens gradually.
Legitimacy is the sense that authority is justified.

passages.q: How can allowing companies to trade the right to pollute reduce pollution?
p: Under a cap-and-trade system, a government sets a limit on total emissions of a pollutant and issues or auctions a corresponding number of permits, each allowing a fixed amount; companies must hold permits for their emissions and may buy and sell them. Those that can cut emissions cheaply have an incentive to do so and sell surplus permits, while those for whom cuts are expensive can buy permits instead, so that the total reduction is achieved at lower overall cost than if every firm were required to cut by the same amount.

The approach was tested in the United States in the 1990s, when a trading programme for sulphur dioxide, a cause of acid rain, achieved its reduction targets faster and more cheaply than many had predicted. The European Union launched its Emissions Trading System for carbon dioxide in 2005, covering power generation and heavy industry; in its early phases, too many permits were issued and prices collapsed, providing little incentive to cut, but reforms that removed surplus permits and tightened the cap later pushed prices substantially higher, and emissions from covered sectors have fallen significantly.

Cap and trade offers certainty about the quantity of emissions but not about their price, which can swing with economic conditions, whereas a carbon tax offers certainty about price but not quantity; economists debate which is preferable and some systems combine features of both. Design details, such as how permits are allocated, whether free permits create windfall profits, and how to prevent production simply moving to places without carbon prices, determine whether such markets deliver real reductions or merely the appearance of them.
g: Cap and trade limits total emissions with tradable permits, so firms that cut cheaply sell permits, reducing pollution at lower overall cost.
The US sulphur programme succeeded cheaply, and the EU ETS, after early oversupply crashed prices, was reformed and covered emissions fell.
It fixes quantity but not price, unlike a tax, and design details decide whether reductions are real or apparent.
k: Cap and trade sets a total limit with tradable permits so cuts happen where cheapest.
US sulphur trading (1990s) succeeded; the EU ETS (2005) had early oversupply, then reforms raised prices and emissions fell.
It fixes quantity, not price (unlike a carbon tax); allocation, windfalls and leakage determine real impact.

mc.s: What advantage does cap and trade offer?
o: It achieves a set reduction at lower overall cost by letting cuts happen where cheapest
It fixes the price of carbon
It requires every firm to cut equally

mc.s: Why did early EU carbon prices collapse?
o: Too many permits were issued, so they were not scarce

mc.s: What is the trade-off between cap and trade and a carbon tax?
o: Cap and trade fixes quantity but not price; a tax fixes price but not quantity

v.d: Surplus permits are more than a firm needs.
Windfall profits are unearned gains from luck or policy.

passages.t: How India became the world’s back office
passages.q: Why did India become a global centre for IT services?
p: In the 1980s a handful of Indian companies, including Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys and Wipro, began offering software services to foreign clients, initially by sending programmers to work on site abroad. Several conditions favoured them: a large pool of English-speaking engineering graduates, wages far below those in the United States and Europe, and the time difference that allowed work to continue while clients slept.

The economic reforms of 1991, which liberalised trade and reduced licensing restrictions, made it easier for firms to import computers and expand, while improving international telecommunications links allowed more work to be done from India itself. Demand surged in the late 1990s as companies around the world needed programmers to fix the so-called Y2K problem, in which older software stored years with two digits, and Indian firms used the opportunity to demonstrate reliability at scale. Rigorous process certifications helped persuade sceptical clients that offshore work could be trusted.

From those foundations, the industry grew into one of India’s largest export sectors, employing millions directly and helping to create a professional middle class concentrated in cities such as Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Pune. Its model, based largely on labour-cost arbitrage, now faces pressure from automation and artificial intelligence, which threaten to reduce the routine coding and testing work that sustained it. The firms’ response, moving towards consulting, product engineering and digital transformation services, will determine whether the industry’s next phase rests on cost or on capability.
g: In the 1980s Indian firms like TCS, Infosys and Wipro offered software services, helped by English-speaking engineers, low wages and time differences.
The 1991 reforms and better telecoms allowed offshore work, and Y2K demand let firms prove reliability at scale, backed by certifications.
The industry became a huge exporter building a middle class, but automation now threatens its cost-arbitrage model, so it must shift to capability.
k: Indian IT services began in the 1980s, helped by English-speaking engineers, low wages and time-zone advantages.
1991 reforms, better telecoms, Y2K demand and process certifications drove growth.
A major export sector built a middle class; automation threatens cost arbitrage, pushing firms towards capability.

o: Automation and AI threaten the routine work that its cost-based model relied on

o: It created urgent demand for programmers, letting Indian firms prove reliability at scale
It was solved in India only

profiting from price differences between markets

passages.q: Can a system that manipulates symbols correctly be said to understand?
p: In 1980 the philosopher John Searle described a thought experiment designed to challenge the claim that a suitably programmed computer could genuinely understand language. Imagine a person who knows no Chinese locked in a room with a vast rulebook, written in English, that specifies which Chinese characters to send out in response to the characters passed in. With a good enough rulebook, the person’s answers would be indistinguishable from those of a native speaker, yet, Searle argued, the person understands nothing; they merely manipulate symbols according to rules.

Searle’s conclusion was that syntax, the formal manipulation of symbols, is not sufficient for semantics, meaning, and that therefore no program, however sophisticated, could on its own produce understanding. Critics responded in several ways. The systems reply holds that although the person does not understand Chinese, the whole system, person plus rulebook plus room, might; others argued that a system grounded in perception and action in the world, rather than isolated symbol shuffling, would be different, or that the intuition the experiment relies on is unreliable for systems of enormous complexity.

The debate has acquired new urgency with language models that produce fluent, contextually appropriate text. Some see them as vivid real-world Chinese rooms, producing convincing output without comprehension; others argue that their internal representations encode meaningful structure and that understanding may come in degrees rather than being simply present or absent. The question remains unresolved, but it has practical implications for how far such systems should be trusted in tasks that require judgement about meaning rather than plausible form.
g: Searle imagined a non-Chinese speaker following rules to answer in perfect Chinese, arguing they would understand nothing.
He concluded syntax is not enough for meaning, while critics offered the systems reply, grounding in the world and doubts about the intuition.
Language models make the debate urgent, with views split on whether they understand, which matters for trusting them on meaning.
k: Searle’s Chinese room (1980): rule-following can produce perfect answers without understanding.
Claim: syntax isn’t sufficient for semantics; replies include the systems reply and grounding in the world.
Language models revive the debate; understanding may come in degrees; trust matters for meaning-heavy tasks.

mc.s: What does the Chinese room argue?
o: Manipulating symbols correctly does not by itself amount to understanding
mc.e: The first two paragraphs set out the argument.

mc.s: What is the systems reply?
o: The whole system, not the person alone, might understand

mc.s: What practical stance follows from the unresolved debate?
o: Be cautious about trusting AI where judgement about meaning matters, not just fluent form
Trust AI fully because it is fluent
mc.e: The final sentence draws this implication.

v.d: Indistinguishable means cannot be told apart.
Syntax concerns structure and rules, not meaning.

passages.q: If markets quickly reflect information, how can anyone earn above-average returns?
p: The efficient market hypothesis, formulated most influentially by Eugene Fama around 1970, holds that asset prices reflect available information, so that it is not possible to earn consistently higher returns than the market, after accounting for risk, by using information that is already public. In its stronger forms, the hypothesis implies that analysing published accounts or past price movements cannot reliably produce gains, because any such opportunity would be exploited and eliminated by other investors.

Supporting evidence includes the difficulty most professional fund managers have in outperforming index funds after fees, and the speed with which prices react to news. Yet challenges abound. Robert Shiller showed that stock prices fluctuate far more than subsequent dividends would justify, suggesting excess volatility driven by changing sentiment, and behavioural economists documented patterns, such as momentum and the occasional bubble, that are hard to reconcile with fully rational pricing. In 2013 Fama and Shiller shared the Nobel Prize in economics, along with Lars Peter Hansen, an award that captured the field’s unresolved tension.

A common synthesis holds that markets are efficient enough that beating them consistently is very difficult, especially for ordinary investors facing costs, but not perfectly efficient, so that mispricings occur and can persist when limits to arbitrage prevent informed traders from correcting them. The practical implication for most savers is low-cost diversification, while the implication for professionals is that any claimed edge should be tested sceptically: if an opportunity looks easy, the first question is why others have not already taken it.
g: Fama’s efficient market hypothesis holds prices reflect public information, so beating the market with it consistently is impossible.
Fund underperformance and quick reactions support it, but Shiller’s excess volatility and behavioural patterns challenge it, both honoured in 2013.
A synthesis says markets are hard but not impossible to beat, so most should diversify cheaply and professionals should test claimed edges.
k: Efficient market hypothesis (Fama, ~1970): prices reflect available information; consistent excess returns are hard.
Support: managers rarely beat indices; challenges: Shiller’s excess volatility, momentum, bubbles; joint Nobel 2013.
Synthesis: hard but not perfectly efficient; diversify cheaply; ask why others haven’t taken an easy-looking edge.

mc.s: What is the common synthesis described?
o: Markets are efficient enough to be very hard to beat, but not perfectly efficient

mc.s: What did Shiller’s excess volatility finding suggest?

Can we borrow to scale it?
mc.e: The final sentence gives this question.

passages.q: Why do people treat money differently depending on where it came from?
p: Standard economics treats money as fungible: a pound is a pound, whatever its source or intended use. The economist Richard Thaler observed that people do not behave this way. They engage in mental accounting, sorting money into separate mental categories, such as rent, holidays or windfall gains, and applying different rules to each, so that someone may keep savings earning little interest while carrying expensive credit card debt, or spend a tax refund freely while being careful with regular salary.

Mental accounts shape many decisions. Money labelled as winnings or a bonus tends to be spent more readily than money earned through ordinary work, a pattern sometimes called the house money effect in gambling; people may refuse to pay for something from one account while happily buying it from another; and the pain of paying seems lower with cards than with cash, because the transaction is less salient. Thaler, who received the Nobel Prize in economics in 2017, argued that these patterns are not random errors but systematic features of how people manage limited attention and self-control.

Mental accounting is not entirely irrational. Earmarking money for particular purposes, such as a separate account for emergencies or savings, can help people resist temptation and keep commitments, which is why many financial advisers recommend it. The cost comes when rigid categories lead to clearly worse outcomes, such as borrowing at high interest while savings sit idle. Recognising which mental accounts serve one’s goals and which merely constrain them is a practical step towards better financial decisions.
g: Economics treats money as interchangeable, but Thaler showed people sort it into mental accounts with different rules.
So windfalls are spent more freely, accounts block or permit purchases, and cards reduce pain, systematic patterns that won Thaler a Nobel.
Earmarking can aid self-control, but rigid categories can be costly, so keep the accounts that serve your goals.
k: Money is fungible in theory, but people sort it into mental accounts (Thaler).

passages.q: Why should a security system remain safe even if attackers know how it works?
p: In 1883 the Dutch cryptographer Auguste Kerckhoffs set out principles for military ciphers, the best known of which holds that a system should remain secure even if everything about it, except the key, falls into enemy hands. The information theorist Claude Shannon later restated the idea as the assumption that the enemy knows the system. The principle underlies modern cryptography, in which algorithms are typically published and scrutinised openly, while security rests on secret keys.

The reasoning is practical. Designs are hard to keep secret: they are shared with manufacturers, operators and users, may be reverse-engineered, and are known to insiders who can leave or be compromised. A system whose security depends on its design remaining hidden is therefore fragile, and once exposed it must be replaced entirely, whereas a compromised key can simply be changed. Open publication also allows many experts to search for weaknesses, so that algorithms which survive years of public attack earn justified confidence.

The contrary approach, often called security through obscurity, has repeatedly failed: proprietary encryption schemes kept secret by their vendors have been broken once analysed, sometimes with serious consequences. Obscurity is not useless as an additional layer, and there is no reason to advertise every detail of one’s defences, but it cannot be the foundation. The principle extends beyond technology to organisations, where controls that work only if nobody understands them tend to fail at the first determined attempt to get round them.
g: Kerckhoffs held that a cipher should stay secure even if everything but the key is known, which Shannon restated and modern cryptography follows.
Designs leak through sharing and insiders, so hidden designs are fragile, while changeable keys and open scrutiny build justified confidence.
Security through obscurity has repeatedly failed, so obscurity can be an extra layer but never the foundation, in tech or organisations.
k: Kerckhoffs (1883): security should rely only on the secret key, not a hidden design; Shannon: assume the enemy knows the system.
Designs leak; keys can be changed; open scrutiny builds confidence.
Security through obscurity fails; it can add a layer but not be the foundation.

mc.s: What is Kerckhoffs’s principle?
o: A system should remain secure even if everything except the key is known

mc.s: Why is a compromised key less damaging than a compromised design?
o: A key can simply be changed, but a design must be replaced entirely

o: The controls are fragile and should be strengthened so they work even if the method is known
They should be made more secret

v.d: Scrutinised means inspected in detail.
Proprietary schemes belong to a company and are not public.

passages.q: Why do organisations stall on decisions, and how can they fix it?
p: Many organisations that appear to have problems with strategy or execution in fact have a narrower problem: unclear decision rights. When it is not clear who recommends, who must agree, who is consulted and who makes the final call, decisions bounce between functions, are reopened after they seem settled and stall while everyone waits for consensus, and accountability evaporates because no single person owns the outcome.

Consultancies and researchers have proposed frameworks to clarify these roles. One, developed by Bain & Company, distinguishes those who recommend a course of action, those who must agree to it, those who perform the work, those whose input is sought, and the single person who decides, and its advocates argue that simply making these roles explicit for the organisation’s most important recurring decisions can speed decisions considerably. Similar frameworks used in project management assign who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed.

Such frameworks are tools rather than solutions, and they can become bureaucratic if applied to every minor choice or if the agree role is given to so many people that it becomes a veto for each. Their value lies in forcing a conversation, before conflict arises, about where authority for each type of decision should sit, ideally close to the information needed to make it well. Organisations that decide well are rarely those with the most sophisticated analysis, but often those in which everyone knows who decides, how input will be gathered and when the matter is closed.
g: Many apparent strategy problems are unclear decision rights, causing bouncing, reopening, stalling and lost accountability.
Frameworks like Bain’s roles for recommend, agree, perform, input and decide, or responsible-accountable-consulted-informed, clarify roles and speed decisions.
They can become bureaucratic or create vetoes, so their value is forcing early agreement on who decides, near the needed information.
k: Unclear decision rights cause stalled, reopened decisions and lost accountability.
Frameworks (Bain’s recommend/agree/perform/input/decide; RACI) make roles explicit for key decisions.
Avoid bureaucracy and too many vetoes; agree in advance who decides, near the information, and when it’s closed.

mc.s: What does the passage identify as the underlying problem in many organisations?
Why can giving the agree role to many people backfire?
o: Each becomes a potential veto, stalling decisions
It removes accountability from the decider

o: Agree explicitly who decides pricing, who must agree and who gives input
mc.e: Clarifying decision rights is the remedy.
